beats.text: A linear inequality can represent a limit on resources. If each item costs three dollars plus a fixed two-dollar charge, staying within seventeen dollars requires three x plus two at most seventeen. Solving gives at most five items.

Now add another requirement: buy at least two items. This produces a second interval, extending rightward from two. Meeting one requirement is not sufficient; a valid purchase must satisfy the budget and the minimum quantity together.

The overlap of the two solution sets runs from two through five, including both endpoints. This compound inequality is an intersection: every value inside meets both restrictions, while a value outside fails at least one of them.

Finally restore the context of whole items. Three and a half lies inside the real interval but is not a permitted whole-item count. The feasible answers are two, three, four, and five, after combining algebraic and contextual restrictions.

practice.answer: Subtract four and divide by five: x≤5.

practice.prompt: Combine x>−1 with x≤6 and describe both endpoints.
practice.answer: −1<x≤6; negative one is excluded and six is included.

practice.prompt: A club needs at least three vans. Each van costs forty dollars and the budget is two hundred ten. List feasible whole van counts.
practice.answer: n≥3 and40n≤210 give3≤n≤5.25; whole feasible counts are3,4,5.

takeaway: Combine constraints by intersecting their solution sets, then apply the context.
scope: Compound linear constraints, endpoints, and discrete feasible values.
title: Linear inequalities
objective: Solve and graph linear constraints, reversing order when multiplying by negatives.
